newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arabs under curfew, settlers roam Hebron streets.
newsitem.headline: Arabs under curfew, settlers roam Hebron streets.

text.p: Israeli soldiers on Tuesday detained dozens of Palestinians in Hebron for defying an army curfew as Jewish settler children turned the deserted streets of the West Bank city into a playground.
Sixty-year-old Hijazi Abu Shakhdam said that his son Wael, 15, was arrested for stepping outside his home into the front yard.
"This is provocation. We are in a detention camp. Settlers are walking freely on our streets while soldiers prevent us from even peering from our windows," he told Reuters.

Israel imposed a curfew on Hebron during last week's fierce clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem. Fifty-seven Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed in the fighting.
During a four-hour break in the military curfew on Tuesday, Palestinians packed vegetable and fruit markets, frantically trying to stock up on goods before being forced back to their homes.
Youths pelting Israeli soldiers with stones were arrested, but soldiers held their fire.
Dozens of Palestinian men and children who remained in Hebron's city centre after the end of the break were rounded up, but Jewish settlers living in the city were allowed to stay on the streets.
Jewish children played freely on the deserted streets in the normally bustling city centre.

"Jews will not leave Hebron. The 50 families living here won't leave unless they're carried out on stretchers. They're here for good," said Mordechai Greenburg, one of 400 Jewish settlers living among 120,000 Palestinians in Hebron.
The city is expected to figure prominently at a Washington summit on Tuesday and Wednesday called to end the violence.

Palestinians want Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to implement an agreement on Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron signed by the PLO and the dovish Israeli government that Netanyahu ousted in May elections.
Netanyahu has said he wants to renegotiate the Hebron deal to safeguard the Jewish settlers who live in heavily armed compounds in the city centre.
Palestinians in Hebron were doubtful the emergency Arab-Israeli summit hosted by U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington would press Netanyahu to implement the deal.
"Netanyahu is an extremist. I think the summit will fail because Netanyahu will not change his hardline policies since he wants war, not peace," said Arafat Daoud.
In 1994 a Jewish extremist gunned down 29 Palestinian worshippers at Hebron's Tomb of the Patriarchs.

Israel was to have handed the city over to Palestinian self-rule in March under a PLO-Israel interim peace deal, but a wave of Islamic suicide bombings that killed scores in Israel last February and March delayed the troop pullback.
The redeployment has been on hold since Netanyahu, who opposed the peace deals signed by his Nobel laureate predecessors Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres, took power in June.

"The situation is tragic. This is unprecedented suffering for us. We hope leaders will not ignore our problem in Hebron during their summit. They have to know that peace will only come when settlers leave our city," said Abdel-Raouf Hussein.
